cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.

cards.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \Sigma\)* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\)* is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in \mathrm{L}(E)\) and \(v\in \mathrm{L}(F), \Sigma *\setminus \mathrm{L}(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(\mathrm{L}(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{h(E):\mathrm{L}(E)=\mathrm{L}\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(\mathrm{L})>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

context_blocks.text: Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma *ab\Sigma *)^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma\)* by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(\mathrm{L}_{0}a_{1}\mathrm{L}_{1}\cdots a_{r} \mathrm{L}_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(\mathrm{L}_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(\mathrm{L}_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(\mathrm{L}(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(\mathrm{L}(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.

context_blocks.text: Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. cards.context:
A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
A ranked alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminal symbols with ranks \(r(a)\in\mathbb N\). Simple types are finite expressions generated by a base type \(o\) and the arrow constructor \(\tau\to\sigma\), associating to the right. A terminal of rank \(r\) has the type with \(r\) arguments of type \(o\) and result \(o\); rank zero means type \(o\). A scheme has a finite set of typed nonterminals, one distinguished start nonterminal \(S:o\), and exactly one rule \[F x_1\cdots x_k\longrightarrow t\] for each nonterminal \(F:\tau_1\to\cdots\to\tau_k\to o\). Here the distinct variables \(x_i:\tau_i\) are the only variables allowed in \(t\), and \(t:o\) is a finite well-typed applicative term over terminals, nonterminals and these variables. Terms are symbols or applications \(uv\), with \(u:\alpha\to\beta\) and \(v:\alpha\) giving \(uv:\beta\); application associates to the left. Rules may be mutually recursive and may duplicate or discard parameters. There are no data tests, constructor equations, pattern matching or nondeterministic alternatives. No syntactic restriction called safety is required.

Starting at the closed ground term \(S\), expose the head constructor by repeatedly replacing a fully applied head nonterminal \(F u_1\cdots u_k\) by \(t[u_1/x_1,\ldots,u_k/x_k]\). When a terminal head \(a u_1\cdots u_{r(a)}\) is exposed, output a node labeled \(a\) with the ordered child trees obtained in the same way from the ground terms \(u_i\). If the head unfolding never exposes a terminal, output a single \(\bot\) node with no children. In particular, unfolding does not require finishing a constructor's arguments before exposing that constructor. This defines \(\operatorname{Tree}(G)\) over \(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). A node address is a finite sequence of positive integers specifying successive child positions, starting with the empty address at the root. A terminal of rank \(r\) has precisely children numbered \(1,\ldots,r\), and \(\bot\) has none. Equality means the same set of addresses and the same label at every address. The number of unfolding steps and the names of internal nonterminals are not observable.

Type order is defined by \(\operatorname{ord}(o)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(\tau\to\sigma)=\max\{\operatorname{ord}(\tau)+1,\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\}\). A scheme's order is the maximum order of its nonterminals; the two input orders need not agree. An input explicitly lists the finite alphabet and ranks, type syntax trees, nonterminal symbols, start symbols and rule syntax trees, with binary indices and delimiters. Well-typedness and the syntactic conditions are effectively checked; invalid descriptions are rejected. The sought machine must work uniformly over all valid encodings, alphabets, finite orders and rule sizes. It returns an exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error, an oracle, or any additional time or space requirement beyond termination.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability of the input language defined above. A positive answer must supply one effective algorithm and prove its termination and correctness on every valid pair, including equal infinite trees and divergent schemes, uniformly in the finite input orders. A negative answer must prove that no total computable decider exists; undecidability for one fixed order already suffices for this unrestricted problem. A positive algorithm only for a restricted order or safety class, model checking of one tree, or a theorem conditional on another unresolved decision problem is not a full positive answer. No finite-depth approximation to tree equality is accepted.
cards.why: This is a central comparison problem for finite programs with higher-order recursion. Their complete output can be an infinite tree, and strong logical properties of each individual tree are already decidable. Deciding equality would establish an effective method for identifying identical observable recursive behavior across different finite descriptions; undecidability would locate a fundamental boundary beyond single-program verification.

context_blocks.text: A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, generated trees have finite-state descriptions and equality is decidable. At order one, equivalence is interreducible with deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. The higher-order setting permits functions as parameters of recursive definitions. Jochems’s §5 explicitly distinguishes this unresolved general problem from the established order-one result.

Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre prove that recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata describe the same classes of trees, with effective translations at each order. A collapsible pushdown automaton has a nested stack structure with links allowing restoration of earlier stack contents. The paper transfers value-tree equality to language equivalence for deterministic machines of this kind, but its final discussion explicitly leaves that comparison problem open. Equivalence of two representation models does not itself decide equality of two represented objects.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems’s 2021 result is a conditional decidability theorem: a specified semidecidability property of coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses would imply decidability of scheme equivalence. These clauses describe relations using higher-order logical rules with a greatest-model interpretation. The required semidecidability remains an assumption in Theorem 4.1, so the paper does not provide a completed equality algorithm.

The same paper proves that allowing explicit divergence leaves does not change the decidability question: its transformation to divergence-free trees preserves and reflects equality. The present formulation retains divergence because it is part of the semantics of an arbitrary input scheme, with no productivity promise. A productive infinite tree and a computation that never exposes a constructor remain distinct outputs.

The April 2026 polyregular result proves undecidability for equality of functions at higher-order types in a calculus with list operations and extensional semantics over function arguments. The paper’s language has no recursion and its programs terminate. Its comparison problem is different from equality of closed, possibly infinite constructor trees generated by the recursion rules in this card; no reduction between the two problems is assumed.

The July 2026 probabilistic-verification result decides almost-sure termination for a type-restricted class of probabilistic recursion schemes. That is a question about a termination probability in a restricted model. It does not settle equality of deterministic value trees at arbitrary finite orders.

cards.definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.

context_blocks.title: Two descriptions of a tree property
context_blocks.text: An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence \(\forall x\)(\(\mathrm{P}_{a}(x)\Rightarrow \exists y\)(\(Desc(x,y)\land \mathrm{P}_{b}(y)\))). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

context_blocks.title: Regular does not automatically mean first-order
context_blocks.text: A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

context_blocks.title: The available relations change the problem
context_blocks.text: A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

cards.definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. cards.formal: Is reachability decidable for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters?
cards.definitions: An input has finitely many locations, clocks initially zero, parameter symbols, guarded transitions and an initial and target location. A parameter valuation assigns a nonnegative integer to every parameter once for the entire run. The algorithm must halt on every finite binary encoding and answer whether some valuation permits a finite run to the target. definitions: A probabilistic automaton is \(A=(\Sigma,Q,\delta,\iota,F)\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), nonnegative rational initial weights \(\iota(q)\) satisfying \(\sum_q\iota(q)\leq1\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \(\delta(q,a,p)\) satisfying \(\sum_p\delta(q,a,p)\leq1\) for each state \(q\) and letter \(a\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.

For \(w=a_1\cdots a_m\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_m\in F\) and \(\iota(q_0)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\). Its weight is this product. Let \(p_A(w)\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \(p_A(\varepsilon)=\sum_{q\in F}\iota(q)\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.

Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \(K\geq0\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \(K\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.

Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.

Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every pair under the two finite-ambiguity promises, or a Lean-checked proof that this promise problem is undecidable. The proof must be unconditional. Restricting one side to unambiguous automata, approximating probabilities, or assuming a numerical gap does not settle this question.

cards.definitions:
An automaton has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), an initial state \(q_0\), and a complete transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\). Completeness means that every state and letter admit a transition; a rejecting sink handles missing transitions. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\) follows transitions \((q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\) from \(q_0\). A parity automaton has a map \(p:\Delta\to\mathbb N\) and accepts a run when the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A Büchi automaton has a marked set \(F\subseteq\Delta\) and accepts a run when transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often. Its language \(L(\mathcal A)\) contains the words with some accepting run. A good-for-games (GFG) automaton admits a single deterministic rule that selects each next transition using only the finite input prefix read so far, so that its induced run accepts every \(w\in L(\mathcal A)\). The rule may remember the entire past; it cannot inspect future letters. One rule must work on all words.

A finite Markov decision process (MDP) over \(\Sigma\) has finite state and action sets \(S,U\), an initial state \(s_0\), a nonempty set \(U(s)\) of enabled actions at each state, a label \(\ell(s,u)\in\Sigma\), and a distribution \(P(s,u,\cdot)\) on \(S\) for each enabled pair. Distribution entries are real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. A policy maps the observed finite history of states and actions to a distribution on the enabled actions. It generates a path by choosing \(u_i\), emitting \(\ell(s_i,u_i)\), and sampling \(s_{i+1}\) using \(P\); products of these conditional probabilities give the path measure. Define \[V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)=\sup_\pi\Pr_M^\pi[\ell(s_0,u_0)\ell(s_1,u_1)\cdots\in L(\mathcal A)].\] In the product with \(\mathcal A\), a policy observes the joint state \((s_i,q_i)\), chooses an enabled pair consisting of \(u_i\) and a transition \((q_i,\ell(s_i,u_i),q_{i+1})\), then samples \(s_{i+1}\) from \(P(s_i,u_i,\cdot)\). Thus the automaton choice precedes that next random state and sees no future. Let \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)\) be the supremum, over all such history-dependent randomized product policies, of the probability that the selected automaton run satisfies its Büchi condition. The automaton is good-for-MDP (GFM) if \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)=V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)\) for every finite MDP over its alphabet and every initial MDP state. The product policy may depend on the MDP. This is exact equality of probabilities, without approximation or a probability-one promise.

Only the automaton is input to recognition; MDPs, policies and GFG rules are quantified objects. States, letters and transitions are explicitly enumerated; indices and priorities use binary integers with delimiters. Input size \(n\) is the total bit length, and invalid descriptions are rejected. The alphabet size, graph size and number of priorities are not fixed parameters. Computational bounds use uniform Turing machines and worst-case resource use over inputs of length at most \(n\), with exact acceptance and no randomized error. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(X\) to \(Y\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) with \(x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y\). A language is \(\mathcal C\)-complete if it belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and every language in \(\mathcal C\) reduces to it in this sense. Here \(\mathrm P\) is deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{NP}\) is nondeterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) is deterministic polynomial space, and \(\mathrm{EXPTIME}\) is deterministic time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked matching complexity classifications for both recognition languages with the specified explicit input encoding and reduction convention. For each claimed complete class \(\mathcal C\), prove the resource upper bound and \(\mathcal C\)-hardness. Any other class used in the answer must have an independent machine/resource or logical definition, not a definition that merely renames this recognition problem or the collection of problems reducible to it. The precision requested is complexity-class completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions, not an exact leading constant in running time. An isolated improvement of one bound, an algorithm requiring a fixed priority count, or a result only for one recognition language is partial progress. Numerical approximation of the MDP values is not the acceptance criterion.

context_blocks.text: Existence of an accepting run is a hindsight property: a nondeterministic automaton can have a successful branch for each word without any single online method selecting those branches. GFG demands such a uniform method. The input automaton is not promised to have the property; recognizing whether it does is the task.

GFM asks a different compositional question. An MDP describes both choices controlled by a policy and transitions sampled from fixed distributions. Its semantic objective only asks that the generated word have some accepting run. Its product objective also requires choosing that run as the word is produced. The second probability cannot exceed the first, and GFM requires equality for every finite MDP.

The policy in the product may be designed for the particular MDP, observing its current state and its past behavior. GFG instead requires one prefix-based resolution valid for every input word. This distinction makes GFM more permissive; it does not turn the two recognition languages into the same problem.

The 2-token theorem settles a major structural characterization of GFG parity automata and yields polynomial-time recognition at each fixed priority count. It does not yield one polynomial-time bound uniform in the number of priorities. The unrestricted input family remains NP-hard and in PSPACE in the checked 2026 survey.

GFM Büchi recognition is already decidable, with a PSPACE hardness lower bound and an EXPTIME algorithm. Consequently the missing result is a matching complexity classification, not an existence proof for some terminating algorithm. The source proves that a qualitative version based on probability-one preservation agrees with its quantitative GFM property, but the card states the original full-probability definition.

The interpretation of “exact complexity” here is the complexity-class classification used by the source when presenting these gaps. Both problems and the unrestricted priority parameter are preserved. Recognition does not ask for a smallest equivalent automaton, and recent minimization or state-reduction results do not automatically classify it.

Existence of an accepting run is a hindsight property: a nondeterministic automaton can have a successful branch for each word without any single online method selecting those branches. GFG demands such a uniform method. The input automaton is not promised to have the property; recognizing whether it does is the task.

GFM asks a different compositional question. An MDP describes both choices controlled by a policy and transitions sampled from fixed distributions. Its semantic objective only asks that the generated word have some accepting run. Its product objective also requires choosing that run as the word is produced. The second probability cannot exceed the first, and GFM requires equality for every finite MDP.

The policy in the product may be designed for the particular MDP, observing its current state and its past behavior. GFG instead requires one prefix-based resolution valid for every input word. This distinction makes GFM more permissive; it does not turn the two recognition languages into the same problem.

The 2-token theorem settles a major structural characterization of GFG parity automata and yields polynomial-time recognition at each fixed priority count. It does not yield one polynomial-time bound uniform in the number of priorities. The unrestricted input family remains NP-hard and in PSPACE in the checked 2026 survey.

GFM Büchi recognition is already decidable, with a PSPACE hardness lower bound and an EXPTIME algorithm. Consequently the missing result is a matching complexity classification, not an existence proof for some terminating algorithm. The source proves that a qualitative version based on probability-one preservation agrees with its quantitative GFM property, but the card states the original full-probability definition.

The interpretation of “exact complexity” here is the complexity-class classification used by the source when presenting these gaps. Both problems and the unrestricted priority parameter are preserved. Recognition does not ask for a smallest equivalent automaton, and recent minimization or state-reduction results do not automatically classify it.

cards.title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.

source_formulation.text: Determine whether exact equivalence of nondeterministic discounted-sum automata over infinite words is decidable.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

cards.why: Exact equivalence is a basic correctness test for quantitative specifications: it asks whether replacing one finite-state description by another preserves the value of every possible infinite behavior. Discounting makes each value convergent but leaves a difficult interaction between exact arithmetic and nondeterministic choices. Resolving equivalence for the basic rational single-factor model would establish a central algorithmic boundary for quantitative automata.

progress.text: The CONCUR paper defines the supremum semantics in §2 and explicitly leaves discounted-sum equivalence open in §3. Its Theorem 3.3 proves PSPACE-completeness of deciding whether a discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function.

Boker’s LICS 2024 Theorems 5.4–5.5 give decidability for Pisot divisor discount factors and suitable algebraic weights. In particular this includes integer divisors, hence reciprocal-integer multipliers here; it does not cover arbitrary rational multipliers.
The LMCS paper proves equivalence undecidable for a model allowing different integral divisor factors on different transitions. A single common rational multiplier is not that model.

The revised target discounted-sum manuscript gives positive results for functional automata over finite words in §6. Its word domain and restricted run values differ from the present general infinite-word problem.

A preprint on target discounted sums computes probabilities for finite Markov chains and studies related strategy objectives. These probabilistic questions do not provide a pointwise equivalence algorithm for the automata here.

sentences: A discounted-sum automaton assigns a convergent weighted value to each infinite run, with later weights geometrically discounted.
Its value on an infinite word is the supremum over all runs carrying that word.
The question asks for exact decidability of equality of two such functions for every input rational discount factor shared by the automata.
Known results for constant functions, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words and transition-dependent discounting have different scopes.
A resolution would determine whether arbitrary nondeterministic quantitative specifications in this basic model can be compared algorithmically.

cards.definitions: Such an automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,q_0,\Sigma,E,\gamma)\), where \(Q\) is a finite nonempty state set, \(q_0\in Q\), \(E\) is a finite set of transitions with source, target and label in \(Q,Q,\Sigma\), and \(\gamma:E\to\mathbb Q\) gives their weights. Parallel transitions, including differently weighted transitions with the same endpoints and label, are allowed. Totality means that every pair \((q,a)\in Q\times\Sigma\) has at least one outgoing transition. There are no empty-label transitions, final-state tests, fairness requirements or restrictions on which infinite runs count. For an infinite word \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run \(\rho=e_0e_1\cdots\) starts at \(q_0\), consecutive transitions have matching endpoints, and \(e_i\) has label \(a_i\). Set \[\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i\gamma(e_i),\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\sup_{\rho\text{ a run of }\mathcal A\text{ on }w}\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho).\] If \(W=\max_{e\in E}|\gamma(e)|\), every series converges absolutely and has absolute value at most \(W/(1-\lambda)\); totality ensures a nonempty run set, so the supremum is a finite real number. Nondeterministic choices are optimized separately for each complete word. No single online strategy is required to select them. All finite sets and transition tables are explicit, and rational weights and the common multiplier \(\lambda\) are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. The deciding machine takes these finite descriptions, not an infinite word as an oracle input. It must answer correctly on every well-formed pair and every allowed factor, without a resource bound. Equality is exact equality of real-valued functions on all infinite words; this yes-or-no decidability question has no approximation tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one total computable algorithm decides the stated equality for every encoded input, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A positive result must handle arbitrary rational \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), unrestricted finite nondeterminism, signed rational weights and all infinite words under supremum semantics. A result for deterministic or functional automata, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words, or comparison up to a positive tolerance does not settle the full target. A negative result obtained by permitting different discount factors on different transitions does not settle this single-factor problem.

context_blocks.text: A transition weight represents a local reward or cost. Multiplication by successive powers of the discount factor gives later weights less influence. The automaton chooses the best run separately on each input word, producing a quantitative language rather than a set of accepted words. Equivalence compares those whole functions.

The source considers total automata, rational weights and supremum semantics on infinite words. Its shared value-function convention is made explicit by supplying one multiplier for both automata. Some papers instead divide the weight at position \(i\) by \(\beta^i\), with \(\beta>1\), and take infima; their discount corresponds to \(\lambda=1/\beta\), and negating all weights interchanges the two extremum conventions.

Convergence does not turn exact function equality into a test of finitely many sampled behaviors or fixed-precision values. The 2023 paper can decide whether one discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function while explicitly leaving arbitrary equivalence open. Constancy is a special case and does not give the required pairwise comparison procedure.

Later results depend sharply on the model. Reciprocal-integer multipliers belong to a decidable family, and more general real-valued Pisot-base results extend that family outside the rational domain. Conversely, undecidability with transition-dependent discount factors concerns a richer interface. Neither result settles all rational multipliers shared throughout a pair of nondeterministic automata.

cards.definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.

cards.title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 2\), is there a deterministic word-RAM algorithm that minimizes every complete n-state DFA over \([a]\) in \(O(n)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: Use a uniform word-RAM with word length w, addressed word memory, addition and subtraction modulo \(2^{w}\), multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by less than w, comparisons and conditional branches, each costing one step. No nonuniform tables are supplied; initialization and preprocessing are charged. Here \(w=\lceil 2 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\). The input gives n, a transition table \(\delta :[n]\times [a]\to [n]\), an initial state and n accepting-state bits. A word is accepted when its successive transitions from the initial state end in an accepting state. The output is a complete DFA for exactly the same language with the fewest possible states. Unreachable states may be removed. The time constant may depend on a; it cannot depend on n or the automaton.

cards.definitions: An input automaton consists of finite nonempty sets \(Q\) of states and \(\Sigma\) of letters, an initial state \(q_0\), a transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and a marked transition set \(F\subseteq\Delta\). For each state and letter at least one transition is present. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\in\Sigma^\omega\) is a sequence \(q_0\xrightarrow{a_0}q_1\xrightarrow{a_1}\cdots\) using \(\Delta\). Büchi acceptance means that transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often; coBüchi acceptance means that they occur only finitely often. Thus \(F\) is accepting in the first convention and rejecting in the second. The language \(L(\mathcal A)\) consists of words with at least one accepting run. A resolver is a tuple \((M,m_0,\mu,p)\): a finite nonempty memory set, its initial element, a deterministic memory update \(\mu:M\times\Delta\to M\), and for each \((m,q,a)\) a probability distribution \(p_{m,q,a}\) on the outgoing transitions \(\Delta_{q,a}\). Its probabilities are arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one; some may be zero. At step \(i\), the resolver observes \(m_i,q_i,a_i\), samples \(\delta_i\) with distribution \(p_{m_i,q_i,a_i}\), follows that transition and sets \(m_{i+1}=\mu(m_i,\delta_i)\). For a fixed word, finite-run cylinder probabilities are the products of these step probabilities; their induced measure on infinite runs defines the displayed probability. The memory size is finite but has no prescribed bound and may depend on the input automaton. Neither the resolver nor its probabilities are part of the finite input. Requiring rational probabilities, a fixed memory bound or memorylessness would be an additional restriction, not imposed here. The automaton and its marked transitions are explicitly listed using binary indices and delimiters; the alphabet is part of the input. Decidability means one effective machine for all such finite descriptions of the specified acceptance type, with exact yes/no output and no running-time bound. The source uses complete automata; missing transitions may equivalently lead to a fresh rejecting sink.
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proofs for each of the Büchi and coBüchi input classes. A decidability proof must supply an effective total algorithm and establish its correctness for the existential finite-memory, real-probability resolver semantics above. An undecidability proof must exclude every total computable decider for that class. A result for only one acceptance class settles only that component of the source question. Checking an already specified resolver, restricting its memory to one state, or replacing probability one by a smaller threshold does not settle either full existence question.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic automaton may accept a word because one successful run exists, even if choosing that run requires knowledge of future letters. A resolver must commit to each transition when the current letter arrives. Stochastic resolvability allows these commitments to be random while requiring failure probability zero on every accepted word.

The order of choices matters. The same resolver is used on every word, but a word cannot react to the random transitions actually taken. Requiring success against an environment that sees those transitions is the stronger adversarial notion studied alongside stochastic resolvability. Probability one here is a separate assertion for each fixed word; it does not require one common set of random choices that succeeds simultaneously on all words.

Finite memory is part of the source definition, not a consequence silently assumed in this card. Memoryless resolvers are a strictly weaker class for Büchi and coBüchi automata. The source also leaves open whether the particular nonzero probability values can always be changed while preserving success, so the definition cannot be replaced by an unproved finite search over transition supports.

The source proves that checking a supplied finite-memory resolver is undecidable for both acceptance conditions. This concerns a pair consisting of an automaton and a prescribed resolver; the present input is just an automaton and asks whether any suitable resolver exists. A failed prescribed resolver may coexist with a successful alternative, which explains why the checking theorem is not already the requested negative answer.

Related positive results help locate the boundary. Recognition is polynomial-time for safety automata and PSPACE-complete for reachability and weak automata. A safety condition rejects as soon as a bad transition occurs; reachability requires eventually entering an accepting region, and weak automata do not mix accepting and rejecting recurrence within one strongly connected component. The unrestricted Büchi and coBüchi conditions allow behaviors beyond these subclasses.

The later quantitative paper studies memoryless resolvers with a fixed success threshold strictly below one. Its undecidability theorem is explicitly separate from almost-sure stochastic resolvability with finite memory. Treating the common word “resolvability” as identifying the two problems would incorrectly retire this card.

Requiring success against an environment that sees those transitions is the stronger adversarial notion studied alongside stochastic resolvability. Probability one here is a separate assertion for each fixed word; it does not require one common set of random choices that succeeds simultaneously on all words.

Finite memory is part of the source definition, not a consequence silently assumed in this card. Memoryless resolvers are a strictly weaker class for Büchi and coBüchi automata. The source also leaves open whether the particular nonzero probability values can always be changed while preserving success, so the definition cannot be replaced by an unproved finite search over transition supports.

The source proves that checking a supplied finite-memory resolver is undecidable for both acceptance conditions. This concerns a pair consisting of an automaton and a prescribed resolver; the present input is just an automaton and asks whether any suitable resolver exists. A failed prescribed resolver may coexist with a successful alternative, which explains why the checking theorem is not already the requested negative answer.

Related positive results help locate the boundary. Recognition is polynomial-time for safety automata and PSPACE-complete for reachability and weak automata. A safety condition rejects as soon as a bad transition occurs; reachability requires eventually entering an accepting region, and weak automata do not mix accepting and rejecting recurrence within one strongly connected component. The unrestricted Büchi and coBüchi conditions allow behaviors beyond these subclasses.

The later quantitative paper studies memoryless resolvers with a fixed success threshold strictly below one. Its undecidability theorem is explicitly separate from almost-sure stochastic resolvability with finite memory. Treating the common word “resolvability” as identifying the two problems would incorrectly retire this card.

sentences: A cellular automaton updates every site of an infinite grid using one finite local rule.
Its ordinary limit set contains configurations that can occur after arbitrarily many update steps from some initial configurations.
The question classifies exactly which two-dimensional subshifts can arise in this way, allowing finitely many transient auxiliary states.
